segments.line: Morning. You open your eyes, and something is wrong with the world.
Above every head, a little label.
Floating. Glowing. Telling you something you were never supposed to know.
The postman at your gate — POLLEN.
The woman pouring coffee across the street — CATS.
The kid kicking a ball in the park — PEANUTS.
You rub your eyes. The labels don't go away.
You check the mirror. Your head is empty.
No label. No word.
Just you, the only person in the whole street with nothing written above them.
You step outside, and the street is full of secrets.
Every person you pass is wearing their allergy like a name tag.
The taxi driver: PEANUTS.
The teacher on her way to school: POLLEN.
The old man feeding pigeons: CATS.
They can't see them. Nobody can. Only you.
What if you could read anyone's allergies?
Not just the worst ones. Every one of them.
All day. Every day. Every head you pass.
Sounds like a superpower, doesn't it? Stay with me.
Because by the end of this, you won't want it.
First, the rules. Rule one: the labels never lie.
If it says PEANUTS, peanuts will put that person in hospital.
Rule two: nobody else can see them.
You can point at the label all day — to everyone else, there's nothing there.
Rule three: your own head stays blank.
You will never know your own allergy.
And rule four: the labels only show the big ones.
The ones that close throats and stop breathing. Not the mild stuff. The real stuff.
So you test it.
On the bus, you sit next to a stranger. His label says PEANUTS.
You offer him a biscuit from your bag — the peanut kind.
He goes pale. He pushes your hand away.
He tells you one bite could kill him.
The label was right. It is always right.
You get off the bus with your heart hammering,
because now you know something nobody else knows.
And knowing is the easy part. Wait until you see what it costs.
What would your label say? Tell me in the comments.
